full_judgment:
K.M. Subhan, J.-This Rule obtained by the defendant-petitioner is directed against an order being No. 54 dated 30-11-73 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge of the 1st Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 136 of 1973. 

 2. The plaintiff-opposite party filed a Money Suit being No. 20 of 1970 which was decreed exparte on 12-8-72. Against this exparte decree an application under order, 9, rule 13 was filed by the defendant-petitioner and the present miscellaneous case was started. The said miscellaneous case was also dismissed for default on 23-3-73 by order No. 46 of the learned Subordinate Judge. Against this order dismissing the miscellaneous case for default, an application under Order 9, rule 9 read with section 151 of the Code was filed by the defendant petitioner which by the impugned order was rejected holding that the application was not maintainable. 

 3. Mr. Saleque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has submitted that order 43 rule 1 (d) provides for appeal only in cases where an application under order 9 rule 13 has been rejected. It does not provide for the situation where an application is dismissed for default. In support of his contention Mr. Saleque, the learned Advocate, has relied upon a decision in Keswardeo Chamria Vs. Radha Kishen Chamria and others, reported in AIR 1953 (SC) 23. In this case on the adjourned date of hearing of an execution case the decree-holder applied for time for giving instructions to the pleader for taking necessary steps in execution but the application for time was refused by the court and the execution case was dismissed in part satisfaction by the very same order without formally calling for the execution case and without intimating the decision in the adjournment application to the decree-holder. It was held by the Indian Supreme Court that the court refusing to adjourn and dismissing the execution case by the same order was a mistake and as such the subsequent order section 151 of the Code, restoring the execution case was proper because on order dismissing an execution case was neither appealable nor revisable. The ratio decided of this case, as it appears to us, is whether an order which is sought to be set aside by an application under section 151 of the Code, is appealable, revisable or not. If an alternative remedy is available or provided by the Code itself then application under section 151 of the Code does not lie. In this connection reference may be made to the decision of Abdur Rahman Miji Vs. Abdul Wadud Mia, reported in PLD 1953 Dac. 183 in which a Single Judge held that section 151 of the Code does not apply where other remedies are available  Mr. Justice Ibrahim in this particular case was considering the effect of a default order passed on an application under 9, rule 13 and whether an application under section 151 of the Code was available in such a case. His lordship after considering a large number of cases of India held that "There is ample authority that section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply where other remedies are available." Order 43, rule l(d) provides for an appeal when an application under Order 9, rule 13 is rejected. The effect of the default order and the order rejecting an application are the same. In one case no reasons are provided whereas in the other reasons are given. In so far as the parties are concerned, the application for setting aside an exparte decree remains the same. 

 4. The scope of section 151 is often misunderstood by the courts below. Section 151 clearly provides for such an application only when the courts found that prevention of abuse of the process of the court is necessary or where of the ends of justice an order on an application is necessary to be made. In the garb of an order being necessary for the ends of justice, in our opinion, cannot negative the remedies available under the Code itself. The appeals or for that matter revisions under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure are provided for to meet situations in which some injustice is felt to have been made to a party to a proceeding. This phraseology for the ends of justice is not an omnibus remedy given to the courts where a final order has been passed to rectify a wrong as may be necessary for the ends of justice. An application under section 151 of the Code, in our opinion, should be used in a limited and in a sparing manner and must be avoided in a case were the Code provides for appeal or for revision.
